initial_requirements: UK fishing vessel masters and owners need an onboard electronic logbook that replaces paper recording for regulated fishing activity. The system should capture required logbook, transhipment, and landing information and transmit compliant reports to the appropriate fisheries administration. It should help vessel operators review and submit accurate records while accommodating relevant data supplied by other onboard systems.
finish_message: All core requirement topics have been successfully completed. The interview is now complete. Thank you for your valuable time and participation!

messages.content: Can you walk me through the main business reasons for replacing the paper logbooks with an onboard electronic system, and what outcomes the new process needs to support on the vessel?

The main reason is to reduce the amount of manual paperwork and the errors that come with rewriting the same information by hand, especially when crew are busy or conditions are poor. We also need something that can capture the required records more reliably and send them on time to the right administration, so the vessel stays compliant without relying on someone posting or faxing paper later.
On the vessel, the new process needs to let the master or operator review what’s been recorded, correct anything before submission, and submit accurate reports with minimal delay. It also needs to work with data coming from other onboard systems where possible, so the logbook reflects the actual fishing activity without extra duplicate entry.
What is the main objective for replacing the paper logbook with the onboard electronic system?

The main objective is to replace paper recording with a compliant onboard electronic logbook that makes it easier to capture, review, and submit the required fishing records accurately. It should support the vessel in meeting reporting obligations without the delays and mistakes that often happen with paper.

When your crew talks about fishing events, catches, and report progress in the logbook, what common words or status descriptions do they use, and how are those terms understood in day-to-day operations onboard?

They usually just talk in very practical terms, like a haul or a set being recorded, a catch being entered, or a report being drafted, checked, or sent. For status, they’d think in terms of whether something is pending, complete, or transmitted, and everyone onboard would understand that as the current state of the logbook entry or report. If there are exact official labels, I’d need to check whether we’ve already standardised those, because day to day the crew tends to use simpler working language.
Are there any vessel- or administration-specific terms for these events and statuses that differ from the crew’s everyday wording, and if so, when should those official labels be used onboard?

Yes, there can be official terms that are more specific than the crew’s everyday wording, especially where the administration expects a certain event type or report state. Onboard, I’d expect the system to use the official labels when generating or submitting records, but still show the crew a clearer working term if that helps them operate it properly. The exact mapping between the two would need to be aligned with the fisheries rules and any terminology the administrations require.

When you move from paper logbooks to the electronic process, what does the end-to-end change look like in practice onboard—from the first record being created through to review and submission—and which parts of that flow matter most to the vessel’s daily operation?

In practice, the crew would create the record as the activity happens, rather than filling it in later from paper notes, and the system should keep it available for review as the trip continues. The master or someone responsible would then check the entries, correct anything missing or wrong, and submit the completed report electronically to the relevant administration. The most important parts for daily operation are quick data entry, being able to review before sending, and having confidence that the submission went through successfully.
Do any historical paper logbooks or paper notes need to be transferred into the new system, or will the electronic record start from the point of go-live only?

My expectation is that the electronic record starts from go-live, but I wouldn’t rule out some need to bring across existing trip or activity information if a vessel is already mid-operation when the system is introduced. I don’t think we’d want a full back-capture of every old paper logbook unless there’s a specific compliance reason. That said, the exact approach would need to be agreed with the administrations and the operational team.
What are the main situations in your operation where the rules affect when a record has to be completed, and what does the crew need to do in each case?

The main situations are usually when a fishing activity happens, when catch is retained or landed, and when anything is transferred to another vessel. In each case, the crew needs to enter the required details promptly, not leave it until the end of the trip, because the timing of the record matters for compliance. If the vessel is still at sea or operating through several events in a day, they’d need the system to support repeated updates without making it cumbersome.
What information must be captured for a transhipment report before it can be submitted?

It would need the essentials for the transfer itself, like the vessels involved, the date and time, the species and quantities, and where the transhipment took place. I’d also expect the report to identify the catch origin and enough voyage or trip context to satisfy the administration’s checks. If there are extra legal fields for gear, approvals, or witnesses, I’d need to confirm those with the compliance team.

Are there any specific rules for the other vessel, port, or recipient details on a transhipment report, such as when those details are unavailable, need to be repeated from another record, or must be captured differently for certain transfers?

Yes, I’d expect some of those details to be mandatory, and some may be repeatable from the vessel’s existing information if the system already knows them. If a detail isn’t available at the time, the process should probably block submission or clearly flag it for correction, depending on what the administration allows. For certain transfers, like where the receiving vessel or port is outside the normal workflow, we may need different validation rules, but I’d need to verify the exact exceptions.
For landing reporting, what information must be present before the report can be submitted?

The landing report would need the landing vessel details, the landing date and time, the port or place of landing, and the species and quantities being landed. I’d also expect whatever trip or catch identifiers are needed to tie it back to the logbook record, so the administration can reconcile it properly. If the landing is handled through a specific market or first buyer process, that may bring in a few extra fields, but I’d want to confirm those rules.

Which fisheries administration or jurisdiction should each regulated reporting event be sent to, and are there any cases where the report needs to go to more than one authority or a different authority than usual?

It should go to the administration that has jurisdiction for the vessel and the activity at the time, usually based on the flag state and where the event happened. There can definitely be cases where the report needs to go somewhere different, like if the vessel is operating in another administration’s waters or the landing is in a different jurisdiction. I’d also expect some reports might need to be copied to more than one authority, but the exact routing rules would need to be confirmed with the regulators.
In what situations would a shore-side person need to review, approve, or oversee a record before it can be submitted from the vessel?

Usually that would be when the master wants an owner, manager, or office person to check the record before submission, especially if there’s a correction, an unusual event, or a compliance concern. In day-to-day operations I’d expect most entries to be submitted directly from the vessel, but the system should allow oversight if the company workflow requires it. We’d need to be careful not to create delays that stop time-sensitive reporting from going in on time.
How should access to regulated records be controlled in the day-to-day business process so that the right people can see or change them while sensitive information stays protected?

Access should be role-based, so the master, crew, owner, shore office, and maybe a compliance user each see only what they need to do their job. People should be able to view and amend only the records they’re responsible for, and anything sensitive like commercial or personal details should be protected from general access. I’d also expect an audit trail so we can see who changed what and when, because that matters for both accountability and compliance.

For the people who can create, review, or submit records, what are the rules for how their permissions change in practice—for example when someone covers another role, leaves the vessel, or needs temporary access to amend a record outside their normal responsibility?

In practice, permissions should follow the person’s current operational role rather than staying fixed forever, so if someone is covering another role they may need temporary access for that period. If they leave the vessel or the company, their access should be removed promptly, and any temporary permissions should expire automatically or be revoked once the cover ends. For amending records outside their normal responsibility, I’d expect that to be restricted and only allowed with a clear reason and traceable approval, but the exact business rule would need confirming.

When the vessel reconnects after a period offline, what should happen to any records that were created or changed onboard while disconnected—should they sync automatically, queue for review, or follow some other business rule?

My expectation is that they should queue locally while offline and then sync automatically once the vessel reconnects, so nothing is lost. If there are conflicts or anything that looks incomplete, the system should flag those for review rather than silently overwriting them. We’d want the submission status to be very clear so the crew knows what has actually gone through and what still needs attention.

When data is imported from navigation, sensors, or gear systems, are there any rules about which readings or fields must be brought in, which can be ignored or edited by crew, and how the system should handle missing, duplicated, or out-of-range values?

Yes, there would be some fields that should come in automatically if the source system can provide them, like position, time, vessel activity, and perhaps catch or gear data where relevant. Crew should be able to edit only the fields that are expected to be completed manually, and anything coming from an external system that conflicts with the logbook should be flagged rather than quietly accepted. If data is missing, duplicated, or clearly out of range, I’d expect the system to warn the user and either hold it for correction or allow submission only with an explanation, but I’d need to confirm the exact validation rules.

Are there any mandated devices or approved platform requirements that the logbook must work with on board, such as a specific type of tablet, vessel computer, or operating setup, and if so what operational constraints do those devices impose?

There may be approved hardware or minimum device requirements, but I don’t know the exact mandated models or operating systems yet. Practically, it needs to work reliably on whatever is standard on fishing vessels, which usually means a rugged tablet or onboard computer that can cope with wet, cold, vibration, and intermittent power or connectivity. If there are official platform constraints, we’d need to align with them because they’ll affect things like offline storage, screen size, and how crew can enter data at sea.

Are there any specific wet, cold, or vibration conditions on board that the logbook must tolerate, such as crew needing to use it with gloves, in spray or condensation, or after it has been left in very low temperatures?

Yes, those are very real conditions we need to design for. Crew may need to use it with wet hands or gloves, and the device could be exposed to spray, condensation, cold, and constant vibration, so it has to stay usable and not lose data. In practice that means the interface should be simple enough for quick entry and the hardware needs to be robust enough for marine use.

For the approved onboard hardware, what practical minimums or constraints should we assume on vessel computers or rugged tablets for offline storage, screen size, and data entry at sea, especially when connectivity is unreliable?

I’d assume it needs enough storage to keep a useful history of records offline for the whole trip, not just a few entries, because connectivity can be poor for long periods. Screen size should be large enough for quick review and entry in rough conditions, so a small phone would probably not be suitable; a rugged tablet or vessel terminal seems more realistic. Data entry should be workable without a constant connection, and any syncing should happen later without forcing the crew to stop and wait at sea.

Are there any certification, approval, or platform-assurance requirements for the onboard devices or software environment that would constrain how the logbook is deployed or updated on fishing vessels?

There very likely are, especially around assurance that the software is reliable, secure, and acceptable to the fisheries authority, but I don’t have the exact certification route yet. My expectation is that updates, device changes, and any software used for official reporting can’t just be arbitrary, because they’ll need to preserve compliance and data integrity. So we should assume deployment will be controlled and any platform changes may need approval or at least verification.
How often do you expect the regulatory reporting rules themselves to change in practice?

Probably not constantly, but often enough that we need to assume periodic updates rather than a one-time setup. In practice I’d expect changes driven by policy updates, seasonal rules, or reporting refinements, and the system should be able to absorb those without major disruption. That’s one reason it would be important for the logbook rules and report formats to be configurable.
In what kinds of situations would the logbook need to be completed or reported immediately, or handled differently from the normal routine, such as urgent incidents or other exceptional events?

If there’s an emergency, a gear loss, an accident, a diversion, or an unexpected landing or transhipment, the logbook may need to capture that straight away rather than waiting for the normal end-of-day routine. Those cases can also trigger different reporting obligations, so the system should make it obvious that the entry is exceptional and guide the user to the required information. I’d also expect it to handle partial completion if the crew have to stop and come back to it later.

When an exceptional event happens, what should the crew be required to capture immediately in the logbook, and are there any specific conditions or limits for pausing and resuming that entry later if connectivity or operations interrupt them?

They should at least capture the event type, the time, where it happened, what was involved, and any immediate action taken, because that’s the minimum needed for compliance and follow-up reporting. If the crew are interrupted, it should save a draft automatically and let them resume later without losing what they entered, as long as it’s still clear that the record was not yet submitted. I’d expect there to be some limit on how long a draft can remain incomplete, but I don’t know the exact timing and would need to check that.

When the vessel has several fishing events in the same day or remains at sea for a long trip, how should the system handle each new entry so the crew can update the record repeatedly without it becoming cumbersome?

It should make repeated entry as quick as possible by carrying forward the vessel, trip, and gear details so the crew only fill in what changes each time. I’d expect a simple flow for adding the next fishing event, with previous values prefilled and a clear way to review the day’s running log before submission. For long trips, it should stay usable offline and keep the entries in sequence so the crew aren’t fighting the system each time they need to record something.

When the crew start a new record at sea, what guided entry, defaults, or templates should the system provide to help them move through the form quickly, and are there any fields that should always be prefilled or left for them to choose each time?

The system should prefill anything that’s already known from the vessel and trip context, like vessel identity, port of departure, and the active trip details, so the crew aren’t re-entering the same information. It should also guide them through the required steps in a sensible order and offer templates for common activity types, but I’d still expect them to confirm anything that can change, like species, quantities, gear, and location. Some fields should stay blank by default if there’s any risk the system could guess wrong, because accuracy matters more than speed for the report.

When a new logbook record is started, which parts of the vessel or trip context should always be carried in automatically, and under what circumstances should the crew be asked to enter or confirm that context themselves?

The system should always carry over the vessel identity, the current trip, the master’s session, and anything already known from earlier entries on that voyage. It should ask the crew to enter or confirm context when there’s any chance it has changed, like a different port, a new fishing area, a new operator on board, or if the system has been offline long enough that the stored context may be stale. If there’s a mismatch between onboard systems and what the crew sees, I’d expect the user to be prompted to confirm before the record is submitted.
Which fields should the system leave blank by default because it should never infer them unless the crew enters them explicitly?

Anything that is compliance-sensitive or can vary by event should be left blank unless the crew enters it, so I’d include things like species, quantities, gear used, fishing location details, catch disposition, and any transhipment or landing specifics. I’d also avoid auto-filling any detail that could be interpreted as the crew making a declaration they haven’t actually confirmed. In general, if guessing could create a wrong report, it should stay empty until the user provides it.

For those exceptional landing cases, what should actually trigger the landing report to become immediate rather than part of the normal routine, and are there any specific conditions or cut-offs that determine whether the crew should use that exceptional path?

I’d expect it to be immediate when the landing happens outside the normal planned landing workflow, such as an unscheduled port, an unexpected discharge, a diversion, or when the authorities require a same-visit report because of the type of catch or the vessel’s status. The cut-off is probably whether the landing is still part of the routine trip plan or whether it has become a separate compliance event that needs reporting right away. I don’t know the exact legal thresholds for all cases, so that would need to be checked against the fisheries rules.

What operational conditions or events should trigger a need to re-assess, re-approve, or re-verify the onboard reporting software after it has already been in use, such as when it is updated, moved to a different device, or affected by a rule change?

Any significant change that could affect compliance should trigger re-verification, especially a software update, a reinstall on another device, a change in the connected onboard systems, or a fisheries rule update that changes what the logbook must capture or submit. If the vessel changes operating area or administration, I’d also expect a check, because the reporting obligations can differ. For minor cosmetic updates, probably not, but anything touching validation, transmission, or required fields should be reassessed.
When compliance-related rules or bugs change, what support or update process should the crew follow to get the issue corrected and the system rechecked before they continue using it?

They should have a straightforward support route to report the issue immediately, then stop relying on the affected function until it’s fixed or confirmed safe to use. After a rule change or bug fix, the system should be updated centrally and then rechecked, ideally with some kind of confirmation that the version is compliant again before the crew keep recording. If it’s serious enough to affect submitted reports, I’d expect the crew to be told clearly whether they need to resubmit or correct any records already made.

Who should be allowed to view, create, and amend regulated records at each stage of the process, and are there any cases where access should differ for the master, crew, owner, shore office, or a compliance user?

The master should be the main person allowed to create, review, and submit the regulated record, because they’re the accountable operator on board. Crew can probably enter supporting details for their own activity, but I’d expect the master to approve any final submission and any amendment to a completed record. Owners or shore office users should likely have view access and maybe administrative support functions, but not be able to change the regulated content unless there’s a formal correction process, and compliance users may need read-only access or audit access depending on the role.

When a new logbook record is started, what context should the system carry over automatically from the voyage, and under what circumstances should the crew be prompted to confirm or refresh that context before submission?

The system should carry over the vessel identity, the active voyage or trip, the current date and time, and any known trip details already established on board, like home port or planned landing port if they’re still valid. It should prompt the crew to confirm or refresh that context whenever the trip changes, the vessel is in a different port, the system has been offline, or any imported data conflicts with what the crew expects. If there’s any doubt about whether the context is still current, I’d rather it ask for confirmation than assume it.

When a crew member is entering or reviewing a record, which specific fields should the system never pre-populate so they stay blank until the crew explicitly confirms them, especially in cases where a best guess could make the report inaccurate or imply a declaration they haven’t actually made?

The system should never pre-fill any declaration-style fields, like catch quantities, species codes, landing destination, transhipment details, discard information, or any compliance reason or exception code, unless the crew has explicitly confirmed them. I’d also keep things like estimated weights, location specifics, and any “final” status fields blank until someone on board has actually reviewed and accepted them. If the system can only guess, it should leave those fields empty rather than risk creating a false record.

When the crew is starting a landing report, are there any exception cases where the system should prefill or carry forward any landing-related details, or should those fields remain blank until the crew explicitly confirms each one?

A few non-declaration details could carry forward, like the vessel, voyage, port context, and maybe the date and time stamp if that’s pulled from the device. But the actual landing-specific details, such as quantities, species, destination of the landed catch, and anything that amounts to a declaration, should stay blank until the crew confirms them. If there’s any uncertainty, I’d rather the system leaves it empty and lets the crew fill it in.

For transhipment reporting, which specific fields must stay blank until the crew explicitly confirms them, and are there any cases where the system may carry forward anything at all before that confirmation?

For transhipment, the system should keep the actual declaration fields blank until confirmed, especially the receiving vessel or buyer, the quantities, species, location, and whether the transhipment is complete or partial. It may carry forward neutral context like the current voyage, vessel identity, date and time, and maybe the last known port or area if that’s just helping navigation through the form. But anything that could be read as an asserted transhipment detail should not be prefilled without explicit crew confirmation.

When the crew needs to enter or check a record in wet, cold, or vibration-prone conditions, what specific interface behaviors or shortcuts should the system support to make quick entry practical without increasing the risk of mistakes?

It should be usable with very few taps, big touch targets, and clear contrast so it’s workable with gloves and in poor light. I’d expect it to support quick selection lists, sensible defaults for non-declaration fields, and the ability to save a draft and come back without losing work if the conditions interrupt them. It would also help if the system gives a clear review step before submission, because in rough conditions people will want speed but still need confidence they haven’t entered the wrong thing.

What operational rule should we use for how long an incomplete draft may remain editable before it must be submitted, abandoned, or reset, and are there any cases where that limit should pause or be extended if the crew is interrupted?

I think drafts should stay editable for as long as they’re still part of the active voyage, but once the voyage or relevant activity has ended, they should either be submitted, explicitly abandoned, or reopened only through a controlled correction process. If the crew is interrupted by poor weather, device failure, or a temporary outage, that should pause the pressure to complete it, but only while the same voyage context is still valid. I’d be cautious about an automatic timeout that wipes work, because that would be risky offshore and could lead to missing records.

When crews are using quick selection lists, sensible defaults, and the pre-submit review step, are there any fields or situations where the system should force an extra confirmation or validation before it allows submission, such as when an entry looks unusual or conflicts with the voyage context?

Yes, definitely. If something looks unusual, like a quantity that is far outside the normal range, a species choice that doesn’t fit the area or gear used, or a port or vessel detail that conflicts with the voyage context, the system should stop and ask for confirmation before submission. I’d also want an extra check whenever required fields are missing, when values were imported from another onboard system, or when the record is being submitted after a long interruption, because that’s where mistakes are most likely.

When crews are entering or reviewing a record in low-light, gloved conditions, what rule should govern when the system can auto-advance or prefill the next field versus forcing the user to stop and explicitly confirm the entry?

The rule should be that auto-advance is fine for purely navigational steps, but only when the current field is low-risk and the next field is clearly dependent on it. If the entry is declaration-like, unusual, or could change the meaning of the report, the system should stop and require an explicit confirmation before moving on. In practice, I’d rather slow the flow a little than have the device race through fields and create a record the crew didn’t really mean to submit.

When a draft is interrupted mid-voyage, what practical rule should determine whether it simply remains open, is automatically paused, or must be resumed and completed in a particular way once the crew regains access?

If it’s just a temporary interruption, the draft should remain open and effectively paused, so the crew can pick up where they left off without re-entering anything. If the interruption becomes long enough that the voyage context changes, or the system has reason to think the draft may be stale, then it should require a review of the saved data before continuing. Once access is regained, I’d want the crew to resume the same draft rather than start over, unless the underlying trip or activity has clearly moved on.

When a transhipment report is missing a required detail at the point of submission, what should the system do in practice to decide whether to block the submission outright or allow it through with a correction flag, and are there any specific cases where that rule changes?

If a required transhipment detail is missing, the default should be to block submission and make the crew complete it first, because those fields are part of the compliant report. I’d only allow a correction flag if the missing item is genuinely not available at sea but the crew can prove it will be corrected through the proper follow-up process, and even then that should be tightly limited. The rule would change only for exceptions agreed with the fisheries administration, or where the system can clearly show the omission came from an approved external source and not from the crew skipping the field.

For the audit trail, what specific changes should be captured and visible—such as field edits, submissions, corrections, deletions, or access to a record—and are there any limits on who can view that history?

The audit trail should capture any creation, edit, submission, correction, cancellation, and deletion attempt, plus who did it, when, and from which device or system if we can tell. I’d also expect it to show when a record was viewed or exported if that’s relevant for accountability, though perhaps not every routine read unless the compliance team needs it. Access to the history should be restricted, with crew seeing only their own vessel records and the detailed audit history limited to authorised owners, masters, and enforcement or administration users as appropriate.

If a crew member reports a compliance rule issue or software bug through that support route, what should happen immediately in practice—should they stop using only the affected function, keep recording in an alternative way, or continue with a specific workaround until it’s fixed or formally cleared?

If the issue affects a specific function, they should stop using just that function and continue with an approved alternative way of recording, if one is available. If there’s no safe workaround, they need a clear fallback process so they can keep the logbook compliant without guessing. I wouldn’t want them to keep using a broken feature unless support has explicitly confirmed the workaround is acceptable.

For the audit trail, are there any specific events or boundary cases we should also capture beyond the usual create, edit, submit, correction, cancellation, deletion attempt, view, and export actions—such as repeated failed attempts, changes made by support staff, or access through delegated or shared devices?

Yes, those boundary cases matter as well. Repeated failed submission or login attempts should be logged, and any changes made by support staff or on behalf of the vessel should be clearly marked as such so it’s obvious who actually did what. If a record is accessed through a shared or delegated device, I’d want that captured too, because it can affect how we interpret the audit trail later.

Who should be able to see a detailed audit history entry for a record that was viewed, exported, or changed by support on behalf of a vessel, and are there any limits based on the vessel involved, the user’s role, or whether the access was from a shared or delegated device?

Detailed audit history for those entries should be visible only to people with a genuine need to know, so typically the vessel’s authorised master and owner, and relevant fisheries administration or enforcement users. Support staff should be able to see the history for the cases they handled, but not access records outside their assigned scope. The vessel involved matters as well, and if the access came through a shared or delegated device, that should be visible in the history, but it wouldn’t usually give extra viewing rights by itself.

When you say the audit trail should capture who did each event, when, and from which device or system if it can be determined, what level of detail do you need for that device or system information—for example, should it record the specific device, the browser or app, and whether it was a shared or delegated device, and are there any cases where that information should be hidden or not captured?

We’d want enough detail to identify the access path, so ideally the specific device or terminal, the application or browser used, and whether it was a shared or delegated device. That helps explain unusual entries later, especially where support has intervened or the crew are using one of several onboard devices. I’d avoid showing more than necessary to ordinary users, and if a device detail can’t be determined reliably, it’s better to leave it blank than guess or record something misleading.

When a required transhipment detail is missing, what should the crew be shown and allowed to do in the system at that point—especially if the omission might come from a genuine at-sea unavailability versus an external source problem or a crew mistake?

They should be shown a clear validation message saying what is missing and why it matters, with the field taken straight to the point they need to fix. If it looks like a genuine at-sea unavailability, the system should let them mark that reason and keep the report in a pending or corrected state only if that’s allowed by the rules. If it’s an external source problem or just a crew mistake, they should either correct it immediately or, if the source is down, use the approved fallback and sync it later.

How often do the regulatory reporting rules typically change in practice, and are there any boundaries on what kinds of updates should trigger a new reporting rule versus being handled as a configurable format or wording change?

They do change, but not constantly; in practice it’s usually occasional updates rather than weekly changes. I’d treat anything that affects what data is legally required, validation logic, submission timing, or which administration gets the report as a new reporting rule. Changes that are mostly wording, label text, or the presentation of the same underlying data could be handled as configurable format changes instead.
